query: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) is an unmodified α + β dual-phase alloy whose low hardness and poor friction and wear properties limit its use under extreme-service and high-contact-stress conditions. Formulate one hypothesis for an intervention that could improve its hardness and wear resistance without sacrificing its existing beneficial properties. State the intervention, proposed mechanism, predicted outcome relative to untreated TC4, applicable operating or test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with an explicit result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Laser cladding a TiAl-based composite coating reinforced with dispersed WC particles onto the surface of TC4 will generate a hard, wear-resistant surface layer while maintaining the intrinsic benefits of TC4.
generation.material_initial_state: TC4 (Ti6Al4V) dual-phase alloy with low hardness and suboptimal friction and wear properties under high contact stress.
generation.intervention: Application of a laser cladding process to deposit a TiAl composite coating containing well-dispersed WC hard particles.
generation.conditions: Testing under ambient and moderately elevated temperatures, under both dry and lubricated friction conditions representative of extreme service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A composite microstructure where the TiAl matrix provides compatibility and adhesion with the TC4 substrate, while the uniformly distributed WC particles form hard secondary phases that reinforce the coating.
generation.mechanism: WC particles enhance surface hardness through solid‐solution and dispersion strengthening; the TiAl matrix ensures chemical and structural compatibility with TC4, preserving beneficial properties while mitigating plastic deformation and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in surface hardness (potentially approaching a doubling compared to untreated TC4) and a significant reduction in wear rate (by an estimated 40–50%) relative to uncoated TC4.
generation.baseline: Untreated TC4 alloy exhibiting its original microhardness and wear performance.
generation.boundary: Performance improvements are expected within the temperature range where the TiAl phase remains stable and under frictional conditions similar to those in high-contact-stress and extreme-service environments.
generation.uncertainty: The exact degree of hardness improvement and wear rate reduction, as well as the optimal WC particle content in the coating, will require detailed experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of TC4 samples with laser-cladded TiAl/WC composite coatings with varying WC contents alongside control samples of untreated TC4. Conduct nanoindentation tests to measure surface hardness and reciprocating sliding wear tests under both dry and lubricated conditions. Analyze coating microstructure via SEM to assess particle dispersion and phase formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiAl/WC coated TC4 samples do not show a statistically significant increase in hardness (minimum 20% improvement over untreated TC4) and a corresponding reduction in wear rate under the tested conditions, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the hardness and compression performance, it can be seen that the 20 WC–HEA composite reinforced with 20 wt.% WC particles has good comprehensive mechanical properties. Friction and wear properties In the research on the wear properties of HEA, most of them increase the hardness and wear resistance of the alloys by adding metal elements for solid solution strengthening and precipitation strengthening, while there are few studies that improve their wear resistance by adding hard particles such as WC. According to the above results, adding WC particles to HEA can achieve higher strength and hardness. Therefore, on this basis, this paper further studied the influence of WC particles on the wear resistance of the composites.

Zhang et al. [] used a mixture of TC4, Ni45, Co-WC, and Y2O3 hybrid powders to prepare a multi-orbital titanium-based laser melting cladding layer on the TC4 surface. The structural characteristics of TiC, TiB2, Ti2Ni, and matrix α-Ti composite phases were investigated. The results revealed an increase in the hardness of the coatings. Additionally, the coatings exhibited a lower wear rate of 47.8% and an average friction coefficient of 10.5% compared to TC4 substrate. The dominant wear mechanism was abrasive wear.
